new_statements.quote: In their phonologies, the East-Central Family languages show a strong development of supra-segmental features manifesting themselves in tonal systems and combined tone-stress systems. The glottal stop phoneme appears with extremely high statistical frequency in the languages of the Gahuku and the Kamano Sub-Families, and in Gimi.

The glottal stop phoneme appears with extremely high statistical frequency in the languages of the Gahuku and the Kamano Sub-Families, and in Gimi.'; p.468 census 'Gahuku-Asaro dialects 23,000 (Gahuku 9,000, Asaro 14,000)'. The passage is about the whole East-Central family and never names Tokano/Lower Asaro, so identity_ok=false; because it offers 'tonal systems' OR 'combined tone-stress systems' without ass…
new_statements.relation_note: Family-level generalisation only: East-Central (Gorokan) languages have tonal or combined tone-stress systems. Nothing specific to Tokano/Lower Asaro; no stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: East-Central Family (incl. Gahuku sub-family with the Gahuku-Asaro dialects) characterised by tonal systems and combined tone-stress systems; no language-specific rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Family-level overview. Tokano is not named; it is subsumed in the census line 'Gahuku Sub-Family 38,000: Gahuku-Asaro dialects 23,000 (Gahuku 9,000, Asaro 14,000), Benabena 15,000' (p. 468), where 'Asaro' covers the Asaro valley varieties (Upper Asaro = Dano dano1240 and Lower Asaro = Tokano toka1244). The prosodic statement is about the East-Central Family as a whole. | Areal survey of c. 25 Central Highlands languages. Table p. 106 lists 'Gafuku (dialects: Gama, Asaro, etc.)' (Gafuku = Gahuku/Alekano; data from Lutheran missionary R. Helbig at Asaroka). Whether Capell's 'Asaro' dialect material is Lower Asaro (Tokano) or Upper Asaro (Dano) cannot be determined; 'Jufijufa/Jabijufa' in the same table is Yaweyuha, not the Tokano alt name Yufiyufa. The accent/tone sentence is a blanket statement for all languages surveyed and is contradicted for Gahuku by later work (Young 1962, Deibler 1976: two tones).

new_statements.quote: Accent is rather variable ; where it does not fall on the antepenultimate, it is marked in the vocabularies and sentences. Some of the languages have a musical intonation ; none, however, employs tone with a semantic significance.

sources.note: For ALEKANO, not Tokano: p. 3 'There are several degrees of stress conditioned by tone. Greatest stress is on a high tone syllable followed by a low tone in the same word. Lesser stress is on a final high tone preceded by a low tone syllable. In a word containing two syllables with the same tone, the first has light stress. Alekano has two phonemic tones.' Not transferable to Tokano without a Tokano source.
